title: Sex Differences in Endurance Running
authors: Besson T, Macchi R, Rossi J, Morio CYM, Kunimasa Y, Nicol C, Vercruyssen F, Millet GY
population: Female and male endurance (road and trail) runners across the reviewed literature
findings: Males and females do not differ in running economy or endurance (percentage VO2max sustained).

Females show a greater proportional area of type I fibres, a greater ability to use fatty acids and preserve carbohydrate during prolonged exercise, a more even pacing strategy and less fatigue after endurance running.
These differences confer an advantage in ultra-endurance, but lower O2 carrying capacity and greater body fat percentage counterbalance them, so females outperforming males remains a rare exception.

Biomechanics differ (greater non-sagittal hip and knee motion in females, partly explained by pelvis width, femur-tibia angle and relative limb length); sex comparison in running biomechanics under fatigue and during recovery is lacking.
limitations: Narrative review without pooling; much of the cited evidence is from small, matched-performance or male-dominated studies. The abstract gives no effect sizes.
implications: Apply no sex-specific running-economy or percent-VO2max-sustained correction to pace or zones; derive zones from the individual's own test, race or wearable data.
Expect similar or better per-session fatigue resistance in females on long runs, but do not shorten recovery or lengthen long runs by sex; no numeric adjustment is justified.
Default ultra pacing guidance to even pacing for everyone.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (Sports Med, 2022-02, first author Besson). Findings supported by Europe PMC abstract (PMID 35122632). Abstract states narrative review scope including thermoregulation and pacing.
